newsitem.title: UK: Germany, France deny planning single EU tax system.
newsitem.headline: Germany, France deny planning single EU tax system.

text.p: Germany and France on Thursday denied a British newspaper report they were negotiating plans to move the European Union closer to a federal superstate by creating a single tax and social security system for the bloc.
Britain's conservative government meanwhile made it clear it would have no truck with such a scheme.

But the European Commission said it could not rule out the possiblity of some form of tax harmonisation among countries joining a common currency. Britain's Independent newspaper said it had seen secret papers in Brussels showing a group of EU states including the two continental giants was working on a harmonised tax scheme.
"There are no such plans by the German government," a Finance Ministry spokesman in Bonn told Reuters.
"The finance and tax policies remain in the hands of member states, even after...economic and monetary union."

French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier, a key architect of the French position in EU institutional reform talks, said he was unaware of any such proposal and ascribed the report to the approach of a general election to he held by May.
"From where I sit, and I am very involved in these negotiations, I can tell you I have never heard of any such thing," he told Reuters in Aubusson, central France.
France, Germany and other EU states have been pressing forward with plans for a single European currency to be introduced at the beginning of 1999.
In London, Prime Minister John Major, his party split on the issue, has refused to say ahead of an imminent general election whether he wants Britain to be involved.
But any suggestion that Britain should cede the right to decide its own tax levels to Brussels would unite all wings of the Conservative Party in opposition.
"There is no question of a harmonised central tax policy being imposed on the UK," said an aide to Major.
He added Britain was not aware of any Franco-German proposals along these lines, which would require the unanimous backing of EU member states to take effect.
The Independent report said the proposals envisage control over income tax eventually being pooled by national governments inside the area covered by a planned single European currency.
It said the tax plans, which were unlikely to have been submitted to the British government, were part of a strategy for a new, "flexible" Europe.
They would be widely viewed in Britain as an attempt by France and Germany to radically alter the fundamental character of the European Union.
"In practice, they are likely to kill off any chance of Britain joining the single currency in the foreseeable future," the Independent said.
A spokesman for the European Commission in Brussels conceded some form of tax harmonisation was possible. "I don't exclude that possiblity...It is intellectually plausible," he said.
The official cautioned, however, that it would be wrong to interpret such a potential development as a further condition for qualification for economic and monetary union (EMU).
"This isn't a new set of conditions that you must necessarily sign up to," he added.
